podcast.title: Licensing of CD Technology (After 1970)
podcast.body: A few years after Jim Russell secured the first patent for his optical recording and playback device in 1970 (which essentially was the first compact disk), Phillips, in partnership with Sony, acquired licenses to further develop this nascent technology into a marketable consumer product. "A few years later, Sony and Phillips purchased the licenses to develop the technology into consumer product."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rejection of Personal Music Player (1972)
podcast.body: In 1972, Phillips, a major manufacturer of consumer electronics, was among several companies that rejected Andreas Pavel's invention, the Stereo Belt. They dismissed the idea of a small, portable cassette player used with headphones, concluding that consumers would not purchase such a machine. "He took his invention to a number of people. Gamahaw, Phillips, Grundig, all big manufacturers of consumer electronics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Compact Disk Development (1970s)
podcast.body: Phillips, a Dutch electronics giant, played a crucial role in the early development of the compact disk. In 1970, Klaus Compaan, working for Phillips, along with Peter Kramer, created the first prototype of a compact disk, initially made of glass, and determined that a laser was the best way to read the encoded information. Phillips and its subsidiaries continued to experiment with this new idea over several years. "In 1970, while working for the Dutch electronics giant Phillips, Klaus and a guy by the name of Peter Kramer came up with a prototype of something called the compact disk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
